artworks.title: East pediment of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia (central group)
artworks.description: In the centre of Zeus's east pediment at Olympia, Oenomaus stands opposite Pelops with Zeus between them — Pausanias' quiet oath before the chariot race for Hippodamia. Carved where the games were held, the king of Pisa is the stone antagonist of the Olympic foundation myth.

artworks.title: Terracotta plaque with King Oinomaos and his charioteer
artworks.description: This Metropolitan Museum terracotta plaque shows King Oenomaus with Myrtilus — the household that races every suitor to death until Pelops arrives. Roman Campana relief keeps the Pisa tyrant's chariot as a portable myth.

artworks.title: Oenomaus and Myrtilus
artworks.description: Relief photography preserves Oenomaus with his driver Myrtilus — the pair whose sabotage (or betrayal) lets Pelops win Hippodamia and whose aftermath names the Peloponnese. The king who killed suitors becomes the fallen father of the Olympic contest.

artworks.title: Pelops mosaic (Noheda)
artworks.description: The Noheda villa mosaic in Spain retells the Pelops cycle — Oenomaus' race still vivid in Late Antique floor art far from Pisa. Iberian reception keeps the king of Olympia's chariot contest as a Mediterranean myth.

popCulture.title: Temple of Zeus, Olympia
popCulture.description: The east pediment stages Oenomaus against Pelops — the race for Hippodamia carved at the sanctuary whose games the myth founds.

popCulture.title: Oenomaus
popCulture.description: King of Pisa who challenged Hippodamia's suitors to a deadly chariot race — father of the bride, antagonist of Pelops, and stone presence on Zeus's temple.
